title: Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams
hook: a grammar teacher comes home from pilgrimage and every word he explains turns into Krishna

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams, through Ramprasad, the clerk who wrote songs to Kali in his account book. Did you plant one small thing in your fallow patch? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-eight.

What happens to a grammar lesson when the teacher can only think of God? In Nabadwip, a town of scholars on the river, the teacher is young and sharp, known for his skill in Sanskrit grammar, and his students are proud to study with him. Then he goes away on a pilgrimage, and comes back different. He sits down to explain a word, any ordinary word, a verb, a root, and somehow the explanation ends in Krishna. The next word, the same. The students look at each other. They came for grammar. Today, the other stream: the Vaishnava stream, and the teacher whose name was Chaitanya.
screen: `A YOUNG GRAMMAR TEACHER.` → `A PILGRIMAGE.` → `EVERY WORD ENDS IN KRISHNA.`

segments.voice: The biographies of Chaitanya tell this story, and they don't make fun of the students. In the end, he closes the school. He can't teach grammar any more, because every word has become a door to the same room. Turn it once. What does he do instead? He sings. With friends, in a courtyard at first, and then out in the streets of Nabadwip: the names of God, Hari, Krishna, sung over and over to drums and cymbals, louder and faster, until people are dancing. That's kirtan, and in this stream it isn't decoration. It is the practice. The name, sung out loud, in company. Turn it again, because the singing could sound like showing off. Chaitanya is remembered for a handful of short teaching verses, and one of them, in paraphrase, says how to sing: humbler than a blade of grass, more patient than a tree, giving honor to others and wanting none for yourself. A tree, the old explanation goes, gives shade even to the one who cuts it down. So the loudest practice in the stream is meant to come from the lowest place. And once more. Remember the conch on the first day of Bengal, the Goddess as Mother? The Vaishnava stream also reaches for a close name. For Chaitanya's followers, the closest of all is the love of Radha for Krishna, and in their stories, Chaitanya himself weeps and longs for Krishna the way Radha does. The scholar who couldn't stop saying Krishna ends up singing in the street, as low as grass.
screen: `EVERY WORD BECOMES KRISHNA` · `THE NAME, SUNG IN THE STREETS` · `HUMBLER THAN A BLADE OF GRASS` · `LONGING LIKE RADHA`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: grass and tree. Sit, and let the breath slow. On the in-breath, picture a blade of grass: low, bending when it's walked on, standing up again. On the out-breath, picture a tree: rooted, patient, giving shade. Go back and forth, grass and tree, for a while. Then think of one person today who might need you to bend, or to wait. If you pray, you can let a name of God, Hari or Krishna or your own, sound softly with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams. Today, the Vaishnava stream in Chaitanya, the grammar teacher who sang the names of Krishna in the street, humbler than a blade of grass. Today's word.
screen: `BENGAL'S SHAKTA AND VAISHNAVA STREAMS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: Bengal's Shakta and Vaishnava streams. Today, in one conversation, be the grass: let someone else be right, and give them the honor without asking for any. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-eight.

screen: `DAY 1378 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: BENGAL'S SHAKTA AND VAISHNAVA STREAMS.`

howItsDone: Gaudiya Vaishnavas, who follow Chaitanya, gather for kirtan, singing the names of Krishna together to the khol drum and hand cymbals, and some take the singing into the streets.

pairs: the names of God sung together

myth: Chaitanya kept his devotion quiet and private
he sang the names of God out loud, with others, in the streets.

and more patient than a tree, honoring others and wanting no honor.
in this stream, kirtan is just decoration around the real practice

fork.setup: you're Chaitanya. you come back from pilgrimage, and every word you try to teach turns into Krishna. what do you do?
options: force yourself back to plain grammar.
close the school and sing the names in the streets.
write a grammar book about Krishna.
fork.reveal: the biographies say he closed the school, and the singing that followed spilled out into the streets of Nabadwip.

trapdoor: what you thought: kirtan is a loud, joyful sing-along.
what it means: for Chaitanya's followers, singing the name together is the practice itself, meant to come from a place humbler than grass.
what a scholar hears: the grass-and-tree verse is the third of the Shikshashtakam, the short teaching verses tradition credits to Chaitanya.

sources.ref: Chaitanya Bhagavata (Vrindavan Das) and Chaitanya Charitamrita (Krishnadasa Kaviraja): the return from Gaya, the closing of the school, kirtan in Nabadwip

notes: Editor pass: hook opener changed (several Bengal hooks opened 'A [place]...'); light wording change in the teach.

The pilgrimage is to Gaya in the biographies; the script leaves it unnamed. Confirm the story of his grammar teaching turning to Krishna and the closing of his school (Chaitanya Bhagavata, Madhya-khanda).

Shikshashtakam 3 paraphrased (trinad api sunichena, taror iva sahishnuna, amanina manadena, kirtaniyah sada harih). The tree giving shade even to the one who cuts it is from the traditional commentary (e.g. Chaitanya Charitamrita Antya 20); confirm.
Chaitanya's absorption in Radha's mood is stated as what his followers' stories say. Gaudiya theology holds Chaitanya to be Radha and Krishna combined; deliberately not stated. A Keeper may want it.
The Kazi episode was deliberately not used, to avoid casting another tradition as an obstacle.
